headline: Pinterest's new terms are live: the 30-day window to opt out of arbitration is open
tldr: Pinterest's rewritten terms and privacy policy took effect Nov 12. You have 30 days to opt out of its new arbitration clause by emailing litigation@pinterest.com.
who: Pinterest users in the U.S. and everywhere outside the EEA, Switzerland and the UK (the arbitration section doesn't apply to consumers there), and anyone who sends messages on Pinterest or posts Pins
seo_title: Pinterest terms took effect Nov 12, 2026: how to opt out of arbitration within 30 days
seo_desc: Pinterest's new Terms of Service and Privacy Policy are live as of Nov 12, 2026. Section 11 moves disputes to JAMS and consolidates mass claims before one arbitrator, with a 30-day opt-out via litigation@pinterest.com.

redline.label: Terms of Service · 11(d) Right to Opt Out
redline.note: Now live. For existing users the 30 days started Nov 12.

redline.label: Terms of Service · 11(c) Mass Filing
redline.note: AAA batches, each with its own arbitrator, become a single JAMS case.

For example, using information (such as Pins, regardless of when they were posted) to train, develop and improve our technology such as our machine learning models and our generative artificial intelligence models.

redline.note: Old Pins are named as AI training material, generative models included.

actions: To keep your right to go to court, email litigation@pinterest.com with your name, account email and a statement that you're opting out of Section 11
Send it by December 12, 2026 (30 days from Nov 12, our count) and keep the sent copy
what:
Pinterest's rewritten Terms of Service and Privacy Policy, first posted as previews around September 1 and covered here on October 20, are now the live versions. Our Nov 13 snapshot of policy.pinterest.com shows the "We're updating our Terms of Service, effective <DATE>" banner gone and the new Section 11 in its place. Pinterest's help page says "changes are effective November 12, 2026" and "By continuing to use Pinterest after November 12, 2026, you accept the updates to the Terms."

## Change 1: The new arbitration section is in force

For everyone outside the EEA, Switzerland and the UK, disputes now go to "binding, individual arbitration administered by JAMS" instead of the American Arbitration Association. The section "applies to any Claim you have not filed in court or in arbitration before the date you agreed to these Terms, and supersedes and amends any prior arbitration agreement between you and Pinterest, including as to Claims that arose before this or any prior arbitration agreement."

Mass claims are handled differently. The old terms sent 25 or more similar demands to AAA batches with "one arbitrator to resolve each batch." The live text says that if 25 or more claimants file similar claims within 90 days or through coordinated lawyers, "all of those Claims will be consolidated into one arbitration before one arbitrator," and the arbitrator may split fees with a claimant's lawyers or funders.

## Change 2: The 30-day opt-out clock has started

The live Section 11 says: "You may opt out of this Section 11 within 30 days of first becoming subject to it by emailing litigation@pinterest.com with your name, account email, and a statement that you're opting out; otherwise you agree to be bound by it." The old terms had no opt-out. For existing users the new terms took effect November 12, so by our count the window runs to December 12, 2026. Pinterest doesn't print that end date.

## Change 3: The privacy policy now says more about AI and message scanning

The live Privacy Policy says Pinterest uses information "(such as Pins, regardless of when they were posted) to train, develop and improve our technology such as our machine learning models and our generative artificial intelligence models." It adds "voice transcripts" to the activity used "to make inferences about you and your preferences," and says Pinterest "may also use, or work with vendors who use automated tools to scan and analyze your messages to detect harmful or unlawful content." It also says connected TVs and other devices "that use our Services" generate log data, and that "Your connected TV may allow you to manage or limit the use of data for advertising."

One difference from our October 20 write-up: two sentences we quoted from the September preview, about seeing ads "when you're streaming a show on your connected TV" and "associating devices that may relate to the same person or household," do not appear in the privacy policy text we captured on November 13. We can't tell from our snapshot whether Pinterest dropped them or moved them to another page.

Other changes: the terms add Pinterest's "GenAI Acceptable Use Guidelines" to the policies you agree to; users outside the EEA, Switzerland and the UK are told their "acceptance of these Terms constitutes your consent to the processing activities described in our Privacy Policy"; and watching YouTube content on Pinterest binds you to YouTube's Terms of Service.

What you can do: to keep your right to sue in court, email litigation@pinterest.com with your name, your account email and a statement that you're opting out of Section 11. Keep the sent copy.
sources: Pinterest Help: Changes to our policies
faq: When did Pinterest's new terms take effect?
November 12, 2026, according to Pinterest's help page. Our snapshot of November 13 shows the new Section 11 live on policy.pinterest.com.
How do I opt out of Pinterest arbitration?

Email litigation@pinterest.com with your name, account email and a statement that you're opting out. Section 11 allows this "within 30 days of first becoming subject to it", which for existing users means by December 12, 2026.

headline: JetBlue makes March 18–31, 2027 peak dates for checked bags
tldr: Late-March spring break flights on JetBlue now carry peak bag fees: $5 more per prepaid bag, $10 more if you pay within 24 hours.
who: JetBlue customers who check paid bags on flights between March 18 and March 31, 2027, typically spring break travel

redline.label: Optional Services and Fees · Peak Travel Dates
redline.note: Late March was off-peak; now it's peak.

actions: If you're flying JetBlue March 18–31, 2027, prepay bags at least 24 hours before departure: at peak that saves $15 on the first bag and $10 on the second
Compare fares just before March 18 or after March 31, when off-peak bag pricing applies
what:
JetBlue's fees page has added a spring-break block to its peak checked-bag calendar. The "Peak Travel Dates" table listed March 2027 as "N/A" on November 12. On November 13 it reads "3/18-3/31". Off-peak pricing still "applies to all other travel dates."

## What that costs

Peak dates raise every paid checked bag. Within the U.S., Latin America, the Caribbean and Canada, the page lists a prepaid first bag at $50 off-peak and $55 peak, and a second bag at $70 off-peak and $75 peak. Adding back the "savings" the page shows, paying within 24 hours of departure costs $60 vs $70 for the first bag and $75 vs $85 for the second. On transatlantic flights, Main Base and EvenMore Base pay $80 vs $90 for the first bag and $115 vs $125 for the second.

Our arithmetic: a round trip with one prepaid bag each way, flying between March 18 and 31, 2027, now costs $110 in bag fees instead of $100; with one bag paid at check-in each way, $140 instead of $120.

What stays the same: the rest of the peak calendar (Feb 11–22, Apr 1–26 and the summer months) is unchanged, and the fees themselves are the ones JetBlue set for bookings made from November 3, which we covered on November 7.

headline: Temu's Dec 7 terms: reject its settlement offer in arbitration and you could pay Temu's legal fees
tldr: Temu's new US terms (Dec 7) say if you turn down its settlement offer and win less, you pay its post-offer legal costs. They also ban AI shopping agents, and the privacy policy drops a no-name-or-email ads promise.
who: Anyone in the US who shops on Temu or has a Temu account, especially anyone who might ever have a dispute over an order, refund or data, plus people who use AI agents or bots to shop.
seo_title: Temu terms Dec 7, 2026: settlement-offer fee shifting, AI agent ban, privacy changes
seo_desc: Temu's US Terms of Use and Privacy Policy change December 7, 2026: lose after rejecting a settlement offer and you pay Temu's legal costs, AI buy-for-me agents banned, an ad promise removed. How to reject by Jan 6, 2027.

redline.label: Terms of Use · Section 19, Arbitration
redline.note: New: say no to Temu's offer, win less, and you cover its lawyers from that point on.

redline.label: Terms of Use · Rules and Restrictions, item 13
redline.note: AI shopping agents join the list of banned uses unless Temu allows them.

actions: To keep your current arbitration terms, mail a letter saying you reject the December 7, 2026 changes to Temu's Arbitration Agreement to Whaleco Inc., 1666 Connecticut Ave NW #500, Washington, DC 20009, USA, so it arrives by January 6, 2027; include your name and the email or phone number on your account, and keep proof of mailing
If you opened your Temu account recently, check whether you're still within 30 days of first accepting the terms; if so, you can opt out of arbitration entirely by mail to the same address
Review your ad choices in the "Your Rights and Choices" section of Temu's Privacy Policy before December 7
what:
Temu has posted new US Terms of Use and a new US Privacy Policy, both marked "Effective Date: December 7, 2026." Each page now opens with a notice that the text shown "is for your reference and will become effective from December 7, 2026," with a link to the version in force today ("Last Updated: November 1, 2026"). The Wayback Machine still shows only the November 1 terms at 06:34 UTC on November 12 and the December 7 notice by 16:37 UTC the same day, so Temu posted the new versions on or about November 12. We compared both documents, sentence by sentence, with the November 1 versions on November 13, 2026. Both are agreements with Whaleco Inc., the US company behind Temu.

## Change 1: Turn down a settlement offer in arbitration and you could pay Temu's legal fees

Temu's terms already require most disputes to go to individual arbitration instead of court. The December 7 version adds an "offer" rule that isn't in the November 1 terms: "In any arbitration between you and us, either party may make a written settlement offer on a claim at any time before the arbitrator issues a final decision on the claim." An offer not accepted within 30 days "shall be deemed withdrawn." Then: "If an offer made by one party is not accepted by the other party, and the other party fails to obtain a more favorable award on the claim at issue, the other party shall pay the offering party's costs incurred after the offer was made, including any attorney's fees and fees paid to the arbitration provider, and shall not recover their own post-offer costs."

In practice, if Temu offers to settle your claim and you go on to win less than the offer (or lose), you could owe Temu's lawyer and arbitration costs from that point on. The rule works both ways on paper, but a shopper with a small claim has far more to fear from a company's legal bill than the reverse. The clause itself says it will be "limited or eliminated" where a law or court decision bars shifting those costs.

Other arbitration changes: anyone starting an arbitration must now disclose "any relationship the party requesting arbitration has with third-party litigation funders" and hand over "copies of all applicable litigation funding agreements"; "all materials and documents exchanged during the arbitration proceedings shall be kept confidential"; and the winner of a court fight over whether the required pre-arbitration steps were followed can now also recover costs incurred "in defending against an improperly commenced arbitration." Two changes help consumers: the arbitration "will be conducted in the county where you reside," and the arbitrator no longer has to be licensed "in the State of New York."

## Change 2: AI shopping agents are banned

The list of things you may not do gets a new item (13): using any feature, "including but not limited to ordering, payments, promotions, rewards, or account management," through "any automated, programmatic, or non-human means (including but not limited to buy-for-me agents, large language model-driven bots, or any end-to-end flow that attempts to place orders without human review) where such use interferes with, circumvents, or undermines Temu's technical measures, security controls, or the intended operation of the Services, except as expressly permitted by Temu." A new item (14) bars framing or embedding "any part of the Services, including any webpage, interface, login page, or form" in another site or app. eBay (February 2026), United Airlines (November 11) and several banks have added similar AI-agent rules this year.

## Change 3: The privacy policy drops its promise not to use your name or email for ads

The November 1 privacy policy says: "We do not use information which on its own personally identifies you, such as your name or email address, to show you interest-based advertising." That sentence is gone from the December 7 version. The section is renamed from "Interest-based advertising" to "Advertising" and now says Temu and its advertising partners may use your information "to serve advertisements and to measure the performance of advertisements shown to you." Ads on Temu itself are now called "personalized advertised listings." The policy doesn't say Temu will now use names or emails for ads; it no longer says it won't.

Also removed: "The merchandise partner will not receive your payment information or device data." Added: Temu may get information from "Age verification service providers"; "advertising analytics providers" are a new data source; affiliates Temu shares data with now include "entities that are located outside the United States"; and Temu may send marketing "via your accounts on messaging applications" linked to your phone number.

## What gets better

The terms add a right to cancel: "you may cancel your order at no cost and without prior notice at any time before it is packed for shipment and obtain a refund," and you "may still return it after you receive it and obtain a refund." The sentence saying a refund "will not cover customs, taxes, or any return shipping costs" is gone from the terms (the Return and Refund Policy still governs the details). Temu can now end accounts "for any legitimate reason," not "for any reason in our discretion." Customer-service calls and chats may be recorded for "service optimization" purposes instead of "training" purposes. Creating more than one account is no longer banned outright, only when it's done to get around the terms, account limits or promotion rules.

## What you can do

Both versions of the terms say that if Temu makes a material change to the arbitration agreement, you can reject it "within thirty (30) days of such change becoming effective by writing to us at the applicable address set forth in Section 18.5." That address is Whaleco Inc., 1666 Connecticut Ave NW #500, Washington, DC 20009, USA, and notice counts "when received." If you reject the changes, the arbitration terms you first agreed to "remain in full force and effect," so the new settlement-offer rule wouldn't apply to you. By our count the 30 days end on January 6, 2027. If you already opted out of Temu arbitration in the past, both versions say Temu "will continue to honor" that. New users can still opt out of arbitration altogether within 30 days "after first accepting" it.

Coverage (checked Nov 13, 2026): searches turned up only Temu's own pages and automated document trackers (TosDiff logged a new privacy-policy snapshot on Nov 13). We found no news coverage of the settlement-offer rule, the AI-agent ban or the privacy edits.

faq: When do Temu's new terms take effect?
December 7, 2026, for the US Terms of Use and the US Privacy Policy. Until then, the November 1, 2026 versions apply.
What is Temu's new settlement-offer rule?

In an arbitration, either side can make a written settlement offer. If the other side turns it down and then doesn't get a more favorable award, it must pay the offering side's costs from the date of the offer, "including any attorney's fees and fees paid to the arbitration provider."
Can I reject Temu's new arbitration terms?

Yes. The terms let you reject a material change to the arbitration agreement within 30 days of it taking effect by writing to Whaleco Inc., 1666 Connecticut Ave NW #500, Washington, DC 20009, USA. By our count that's by January 6, 2027. Your earlier arbitration terms would then still apply.
Does Temu ban AI shopping agents?

From December 7, yes, where they interfere with or get around Temu's technical measures, security controls or the intended operation of the service: the terms name "buy-for-me agents, large language model-driven bots" and order flows "without human review," unless Temu expressly permits them.
Will Temu use my name or email for ads?

The new privacy policy doesn't say it will. It removes the old sentence saying Temu does not use information that on its own identifies you, "such as your name or email address," to show you interest-based ads.
